name: Schloss Lichtenwerth
kurzbeschreibung: Schloss Lichtenwerth in Münster: North Tyrol's only preserved late-Romanesque moated castle from the 12th century, idyllically surrounded by reed ponds along the Inn.
beschreibung:
Overview

Dreamlike Schloss Lichtenwerth (also known as Burg Lichtwerth or Lichtenwörth) is situated in the municipality of Münster near Brixlegg in the Tyrolean Unterinntal. Set on a former river island on the north bank of the Inn River, the complex represents a cultural-historical rarity of European stature: it is the only preserved late-Romanesque moated water castle in all of North Tyrol. While most Tyrolean castles perch boldly on craggy rocky promontories as defensive hill fortresses, Lichtenwerth nestles picturesquely into the riverside alluvial forest, reflecting its defiant stone walls in a tranquil, waterlily-covered moat.

History & Architecture

The name of the fortification derives from the Middle High German term “Wörth” or “Werth”, signifying a river island. The stronghold was erected in the early 12th century at a strategic former side arm of the Inn River to control lucrative shipping traffic, tolls, and the crucial river crossing. Early documentary mentions date to 1212 and 1249 as a seat of ministerial nobles of the Archbishopric of Salzburg and the powerful Herren von Freundsberg. Following the extinction of the Freundsberg family, the water fortress passed into the possession of the Tyrolean sovereigns in the 14th century; both Herzog Friedrich IV. and Sigmund der Münzreiche stayed here. In the 16th century, the Schwaz mining entrepreneur family Mornauer acquired the castle, followed later by the noble dynasties Kirchmayr and Sterzinger. In 1879, the eminent political scientist and statistician Karl Theodor von Inama-Sternegg purchased the historic estate. To this day, the castle remains in the private possession of his descendants, who carefully preserve the ensemble. The architecture is distinguished by its two-part layout: an extensive outer bailey with farm buildings and stables, and the compact inner castle with its striking four-storey Romanesque keep (Bergfried) and Late Gothic palace building. Inside, the castle conceals cultural treasures, including a completely preserved Gothic castle kitchen, a Rococo chapel dating from 1776, and an intact private baroque court theatre from 1765 with hand-painted stage sets.

Visit & Getting There

As Schloss Lichtenwerth is privately owned and inhabited year-round, its interior rooms and castle courtyard are not open to the public (no interior tours). However, the exterior grounds, defensive walls, and surrounding moat can be viewed freely and completely free of charge (admission €0.00) at any time of year on a stroll along public paths. Arrival by public transport: by train (ÖBB) to Bahnhof Brixlegg; from there, a flat, scenic walking route leads across the Inn bridge and along the Inntal cycle path in about 15 minutes (approx. 1.2 km) directly to the castle grounds. Alternatively, take VVT bus line 601 to the stop Münster Grünsbach. By car: via the Inntalautobahn A12, exit Kramsach/Brixlegg, then continue along the B171 Tiroler Straße approx. one kilometre west of Brixlegg; parking is available at the nearby visitor car park of Schlosspark Matzen (approx. 400 metres' walk).

Tips

The waterside path along the castle pond is completely level, paved or fine gravel, and ideally suited for wheelchairs, seniors, and prams. Schloss Lichtenwerth forms a fascinating castle quadrangle together with Schloss Matzen, Schloss Neumatzen, and the Ruine Kropfsberg ruins. Be sure to combine your photo stop with a leisurely walk through the publicly accessible English landscape garden of Schloss Matzen with its ancient giant trees and romantic ponds. The reflection of the Romanesque keep in the reed-fringed pond makes an extraordinary photo motif in the early morning light.
